terms.grammar: imperative of afferō with the dative; nōbīs for “us”; add quaesō or sīs to make it a request
evidence: Ter. Haut. 223: «dā mihi» atque «adfer mihi»
Hor. Epod. 9.33: capāciōrēs adfer hūc, puer, scyphōs
terms.comment: Latin asks for things to be brought with the plain imperative, softened by quaesō or sīs; Clitipho in Terence groans at his girl’s “give me” and “bring me”. Our own Latin writes the assimilated affer; the quotations keep their edition’s adfer. For a thing within reach, Cedo … (see “give it here!”).

evidence: Ter. Haut. 223: «dā mihi» atque «adfer mihi»

phrases.latin: Affer nōbīs, quaesō, aquam et pānem.
phrases.english: Could we have some water and bread, please?

phrases.latin: Dā mihi, sīs, alteram furcillam; haec cecidit.
phrases.english: Could I have another fork, please? This one fell on the floor.

phrases.latin: capāciōrēs adfer hūc, puer, scyphōs et Chīa vīna aut Lesbia
phrases.english: bring larger cups here, boy, and Chian or Lesbian wine

phrases.latin: mage nunc mē amīcae dicta stimulant «dā mihi» atque «adfer mihi»
phrases.english: what goads me now is my girlfriend’s “give me” and “bring me”
Can I have some water, please? I’m thirsty.
